name: Easter

attributes.attribute: kept on different dates by insular and Roman churches
dispute over the date of Easter among the Celtic churches
664 council that settled Northumbria on the Roman reckoning
took over spring rites such as the dancing sun and holy well cures

sources: MacNeill, Máire. The Festival of Lughnasa, Parts I and II. Dublin: Comhairle Bhéaloideas Éireann, 1982.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Easter is a Christian feast that reached the Celtic lands, where it stood alongside the older spring festival. In early Ireland and Britain the churches argued for over a century over the date on which to keep it, a dispute known as the Easter controversy. Koch 2006 explains that the Britons and Irish used an older 84-year cycle, while the Roman church used a 19-year cycle. To medieval minds Easter marked the yearly victory of light over darkness, so to date it wrongly was to misunderstand creation. St Patrick followed the Alexandrian computus of the Roman type. Around 600 the Irish monk Columbanus wrote to Pope Gregory defending the insular Easter. In 664 the Synod of Whitby settled the question for Northumbria, which took the Roman reckoning, and the Irish abbot Colmán withdrew to Ireland. Iona came into line in 716, and St Elfoddw changed the reckoning in Wales in 768. In Irish folk custom Easter took over spring rites, so that people said the sun danced on Easter morning and held the holy wells more potent for cures then. Some folk tales even set the great fires of the old season on Easter.

okr.objective: Document Easter and the Easter controversy in the Celtic lands, from Koch 2006.
key_results: The insular churches used an older 84-year cycle, the Roman church a 19-year cycle.
Columbanus defended the insular Easter in letters to Pope Gregory around 600.
The Synod of Whitby in 664 set Northumbria on the Roman reckoning.
